newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House votes reprimand, big fine for Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House votes reprimand, big fine for Gingrich.

text.p: In a historic and humbling rebuke to its leader, the U.S. House of Representatives voted on Tuesday to reprimand Speaker Newt Gingrich and slap him with a $300,000 penalty for ethics violations.
The action made Gingrich, 53, a Georgia Republican, the first House speaker in U.S. history to be punished for misconduct by formal vote of his colleagues.

"The penalty is tough and unprecedented," Representative Nancy Johnson, Republican chairwoman of the ethics committee that recommended the penalties, said in debate. "It is also appropriate. No one is above the rules of the House of Representatives."

Gingrich admitted last December that he failed to get proper legal advice on the use of tax-exempt funds to finance a lecture course critics called partisan politics, and to misinforming House investigators on the facts of that case.
A House ethics report concluded, and Gingrich conceded, that conduct had brought discredit upon the House.
The vote climaxed two years of bitter political strife focused on the speaker and members of the ethics committee.

Gingrich was re-elected speaker just two weeks ago in a close vote in which a few of his own party party members deserted him. He is the third-highest elected official of the United States after the president and vice president.

In reporting the matter to the House with its recommendations for punishment, which were those approved on Tuesday, the ethics committee said the offence called for a penalty "somewhere in between" a reprimand and the more serious censure. The latter would have almost certainly required Gingrich to step down.
Recent opinion polls have suggested Gingrich is one of the most unpopular politicians in the United States, with only about a third of Americans approving of the job he is doing.
Gingrich appeared before House Republicans in a closed party caucus on Tuesday morning before the vote.
Some Republicans emerging from the meeting voiced concern at the monetary penalty. Representative Bill McCollum of Florida, said. "This $300,000 is wrong. Any amount of money is wrong."

Republican Sherwood Boehlert of New York, said the penalty set a dangerous precedent. "Any one of us could be charged with some kind of inadvertent act... it really sets a very dangerous precedent," he said.

Representative David McIntosh of Indiana said the size of the penalty "surprised everyone" and had sparked discussion of a "loser pays" proposal under which members filing complaints that were dismissed would pay towards the cost of the investigation.

The Gingrich ethics case has been the subject of fierce political jockeying. But as the vote approached both Republicans and Democrats said they wanted to get the vote on his punishment behind them and return to working on issues such as a balanced budget and social programmes.
One of the major themes of President Bill Clinton's inaugural address on Monday was a call for bipartisan cooperation between the Republican-controlled Congress and the Democratic White House.

Speaking on NBC's "Today" show early on Tuesday, Johnson, a Connecticut Republican, said one of the reasons for the committee's verdict "is to try to put this era of animosity and divisiveness and partisanship behind the House."
